title: Mullin Opens Door to DACA Deal in Congress, Rules Out Amnesty
excerpt: The DHS secretary said Trump told him to work with Democrats on immigration legislation and that Congress could weigh permanent status for DACA recipients — with enforcement policy unchanged and no bill yet introduced.
body:
• Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Monday that President Trump has told him to start working with Democrats who have reached out about immigration legislation in the new Congress.
  • Mullin suggested Congress could create a path for DACA recipients to become "maybe legal permanent citizens," while insisting: "We're never going to allow amnesty to happen."
  • Nothing has changed in enforcement policy, and no bill exists yet — any permanent status for DACA recipients requires an act of Congress, not DHS.
  • About 455,200 people held active DACA status at the end of March 2026, according to USAFacts' compilation of USCIS data.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Monday that President Donald Trump has encouraged him to work with Democrats who have reached out about immigration reform, and that Congress could consider a pathway to permanent legal status for recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals — while ruling out amnesty and any change to enforcement policy, Fox News reported.

Who is affected — and who is not

The comments concern DACA recipients: immigrants brought to the United States illegally as children who hold temporary protection from deportation and work authorisation under the Obama-era programme. About 455,200 people held active DACA status at the end of March 2026, according to USAFacts, which compiles US Citizenship and Immigration Services data. Mullin did not extend the suggestion to any other group, and he emphasised that he and Trump have not discussed changing the administration's enforcement policies. "But has there been a conversation about changing the policy?" Mullin said of his discussions with Trump. "No, we haven't had that conversation."

"We're never going to allow amnesty to happen."

— Markwayne Mullin, US Homeland Security Secretary

What Mullin actually proposed

Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a counter-drone conference in Maryland, Mullin said "a lot of Democrats" have contacted him about working together on immigration legislation in the new Congress. "I've let the president know that those calls are coming in, and the president has said, 'Let's start working with them and then let's meet at some point,'" Mullin said. On DACA specifically, he framed any change as Congress's decision, not his department's:

"If we want to have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that'll be up to Congress."

— Markwayne Mullin, US Homeland Security Secretary

The distinction matters legally. DACA is deferred action — a decision not to pursue removal, plus a work permit. It is not a lawful status, a point DHS itself made in a March post on X stating that DACA "does not confer any form of legal status in this country." Only legislation can convert that temporary protection into permanent residence; a green card, in turn, is separate from citizenship, which comes later through naturalisation. The Fox News report of Mullin's remarks and the Immigration Analytics explainer both stress that no bill has been introduced.

A shift in tone from the same department

Mullin's willingness to discuss a legislative pathway marks a shift in tone from his department's messaging earlier this year. In its March post, DHS warned that recipients could be arrested and deported, including for criminal conduct, and said ICE arrested 264 DACA recipients nationwide between January 20 and September 28, 2025, more than 92% of whom had been charged with or convicted of a crime in the United States. Monday's comments were Mullin's first public suggestion that DACA recipients could gain permanent legal status through congressional action. DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment by publication time.

What to do next

For DACA recipients, the correct action today is nothing new: there is no application, form or filing opened by these remarks, and renewals continue under the existing programme rules. What to watch is whether a bill is actually introduced when the new Congress organises, and whether the White House attaches conditions — enforcement funding or eligibility cut-offs — that decide whether Mullin's opening becomes legislation or remains a negotiating signal.
